newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico City fire snuffed out, four dead.
newsitem.headline: Mexico City fire snuffed out, four dead.

text.p: Firefighters on Wednesday finally snuffed out a deadly blaze in three fuel tanks two days after they exploded outside Mexico City, killing four people, officials said.
Charred, burgundy-tinted remains of two giant fuel tanks and one smaller one stood as a grim reminder of the inferno, which hospitalized 19 people and destroyed more than 100,000 barrels of gasoline.

Workers from Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) and its insurer began to examine the damaged hulks of the tanks for clues as to what caused the fire, which began when Pemex workers were repairing a leaky valve on one of the tanks.
At least 16 people were injured in the disaster, which produced a raging fireball and a column of black smoke billowing three miles (five km) into the sky above this city of 18 million.
Two Pemex workers died early on Wednesday from their burns, following another Pemex worker and a fireman who died on Tuesday in the accident.
As more than 5,000 evacuees from the northern Mexico City suburb San Juan Ixhuatepec returned to their homes, Mexican opposition congressmen demanded that Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous resign.

Pemex, the world's fifth largest oil company, has had a string of fatal disasters in recent years, including a 1992 leak that blew up whole streets and killed more than 200 people in Mexico's second largest city, Guadalajara.

"(Lajous) must leave Pemex," left-wing Senator Felix Salgado Macedonio said. "It is not right that he is still being kept in that job; ineptitude, incompetence and corruption is rampant in Pemex," he said.

"This accident is not only painful but frankly outrageous," added environmental group Greenpeace in a statement on Tuesday. "Pemex's accidents are much more frequent and serious than other oil companies around the world."
Lajous told reporters he would stay on as head of Pemex.

"If my resignation would serve to improve the operating efficiency of Pemex or would serve to improve the security of our installations, I would seriously consider that possibility. I don't believe it would," he said.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, who is currently on a trip to Buenos Aires, called for increased safety measures at oil installations following the disaster.
"We are calling on specialists to give recommendations to boost safety measures and reduce (the possibility of accidents) to practically zero," Zedillo said.
Discussing the accident with reporters, Lajous noted that a Texaco refinery in Los Angeles, California had suffered a larger fire the same day as the Mexico blast.
"This does not excuse the incident...but the petroleum industry assumes certain risks not just here, but in the whole world," Lajous said.
The Pemex chairman has accepted responsibility for the incident, and pledged greater attention to security and training within the company.
